extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for determining what subject-matter is patentable (manufactures, machines, processes, compositions, arts) and for construing the scope of patent claims (what the patentee actually appropriated versus public domain). Includes tests, presumptions, and examples from English and U.S. practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of laws, properties, or qualities of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth, law, property, or quality of matter, or laws of physics, being common property, may be appropriated only insofar as they are applied in the subject with which, the means by which, and the end for which the inventor has applied them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor does not monopolize a law of nature itself; the patent 'appropriates' the law only to the extent that its application (to a subject, by particular means, for a particular end) enters into the essence of the invention. The extent of appropriation is measured by applications which, according to law and logic, would be deemed piracy of the original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence or substance of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a law, property, or quality of matter to a subject by particular means for a particular end 'constitutes the essence and substance of the invention' and is what the patentee has invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What the patentee actually invented (the essence) cannot be taken from him without violating the principles of property in invention; this essence is the primary measure when construing claims and determining scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, arrangement, or apparatus immaterial when not part of essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where form, arrangement of matter, proportion, method of construction, or apparatus employed are not of the essence of the invention, changes in them that do not change the characteristic or purpose of the invention are immaterial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention's characteristic persists through variations of form or apparatus, substituting equivalents that do not change the principle amounts merely to different modes of practising the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution by equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same effect of a mechanism can be produced by substituting a different contrivance which does not change the characteristic of the machine, such substitution is only a different mode of practising the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent substitutions are encompassed by a patent when they do not change the characteristic, essence, or principle of the invention; this is illustrated especially in machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as a contract between patentee and the public; two focal questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent should be construed as a contract or bargain between the patentee and the public on points involving rights and interests: (1) the extent of the claim, and (2) the intelligibility of the description for purposes of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of the claim is generally a question for the court; the sufficiency/intelligibility of the description for practice is generally a question for the jury under court direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test for whether old matter is included in a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether the patentee has included in his claim something not new, ascertain (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first is an evidentiary question (is the thing old?), the second is a question of construction (does the claim language include it?). If the public is misled, the patent ought not to stand; but construction should be fair to reach just import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in doubtful cases: construe in favor of the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after applying rules of construction, doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, the patentee is to be presumed to have intended to claim no more than he actually invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud is not to be presumed; the maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat guides courts to support a claim if it can be done without violating principle. This presumption operates only in doubtful cases and not where a claim is manifestly too broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrictive construction to make claim coextensive with actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should be construed so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual invention, if this can be done consistently with legal principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule helps preserve the patent for the real invention (patent may remain valid pro tanto) but will not save claims that clearly attempt to appropriate more than was invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: No monopoly beyond the fair fruits of actual invention (policy principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law establishes no monopoly beyond the fair fruits of actual invention; it protects the real inventor in enjoyment of what he first produced, while encouraging inventive labor as public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy underlies liberal construction in favor of patentees in many decisions but also limits patents to real contributions: new characteristics, results, or advantages not embraced by former inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and scope of 'manufacture' and related statutory terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory term 'manufacture' has been construed broadly to include both tangible products and, figuratively, the mode of producing a thing or an effect; the patent statute also uses 'art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'manufacture' may literally mean something made by hand or be extended to include new processes, modes of practice, or results attained by art or skill. Recent statutes using 'inventions' assume this settled construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of principles vs. their practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere principle (an abstract discovery) is not patentable as a 'manufacture'; but a principle that is embodied and connected with corporeal substances or a mode of using it so as to act and produce effects becomes a patentable process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Watt's invention (practical means of lessening steam consumption) exemplifies carrying a principle into a practical process and machine; courts sustain patents for applied principles, not for bare abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to claim product versus method/process
rubrics_metrics.description: If the effect produced is a new substance or composition, the proper privilege is for the new substance itself; if the effect is not a substance (e.g., arrangement producing a negative quality), the patent should be for the method or mechanism by which the effect is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents for methods of producing known articles may be proper where the article itself is not distinguishably new but the process is (e.g., dyeing methods); conversely, when a new object is produced, claim the object where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes and methods as patentable 'manufactures' or 'arts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes, methods, or practical applications of principles that produce useful effects are within the statutory subjects of patents (art, manufacture, machine, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'art' was selected to embrace inventions where particular apparatus or materials are not the essence but the mode of using them is new—covering new methods of producing results, improved economy, speed, or simplicity in industry (illustrated by Hartley's and other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction balancing: protect public from misleading claims vs. protect inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If the public has been misled by a claim (e.g., patentee represents he invented something that existed before), the patent ought not to stand; yet courts should not adopt constructions that destroy a patent lightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply fair construction to reach the just import; where no doubt exists that the claim is manifestly broader than the invention, the patent may be invalidated; otherwise prefer an interpretation that preserves the real invention.
